title: Capturing AI-Assistant Referrers in Application Logs Without Breaking Caching
author: Peter Panda
summary: When a user clicks from an AI answer into your site, the referrer field is one of the few signals you get. Many teams lose it to CDN defaults, aggressive cache keys or SPA navigations that never send the first landing referrer to analytics. Log the first HTML request In nginx (or your edge worker), dump $http_referer , $arg_utm_source and a request id on the first document request. Do not wait for a tag manager event; ad blockers and refused JS wipe that path. Keep HTML cache keys from ignoring the landing URL If you cache HTML, ensure the first landing still records referrer server-side before a cache hit serves a shell. Some stacks log only on miss; force a lightweight collect endpoint instead. Normalise known assistant hosts Maintain a small map: host contains chatgpt , perplexity , copilot , etc. Store both raw referrer and a normalised ai_source dimension so dashboards stay readable when domains change. Pass the signal into the CRM on form submit Stash the first referrer in a first-party cookie or server session with a short TTL. On lead submit, write it onto the contact. Otherwise sales never sees that the lead came from an assistant. Review weekly, not once a quarter AI traffic patterns shift. A weekly count of landings by ai_source is enough to see whether content experiments move anything. Practical checklist Before you ship the change, walk through a short checklist with someone who did not write the page. Ask them to explain the offer, the price or fee range, the timeline and the main risk in their own words. If they cannot, the draft is not ready for assistants or for humans either. Document the owner of the page, the next review date and the source of every number you quote. When a platform policy or a fee changes, you want a single place to update rather than a scavenger hunt across blog posts, help articles and sales decks. Common failure modes Teams usually fail in three ways. They publish once and never revisit dates. They keep conflicting facts on the About page, a directory and a PDF one-pager. They measure vanity traffic instead of whether the answers that matter improved. A lightweight monthly review catches all three earlier than a panicked quarterly audit. How this ties to pandawm.com work Overseas ads, multilingual sites, GEO and crypto checkout for overseas merchants share the same underlying need: clear facts, consistent entities and pages that can be quoted without guesswork. The implementation details differ by channel; the editorial discipline does not. A fuller attribution pattern for AI leads is in how to attribute AI search leads . Published by PandaWM , an overseas marketing team based in Hong Kong.

title: A Robots.txt Matrix for AI Crawlers: Allow, Delay or Block by Bot
author: Peter Panda
summary: Different AI crawlers honour robots.txt in different ways, and a single Disallow: / aimed at one vendor can accidentally silence another that your GEO programme cares about. A small matrix in version control beats tribal knowledge in Slack. Inventory the bots you actually see From two weeks of access logs, list user-agents that look like AI or training crawlers. Common ones change over time, so do not copy a blog post from last year blindly. Note path volume and status codes for each. Decide per bot, not globally For each bot, pick one policy: allow all public content, allow only /blog and docs, crawl-delay if supported, or block. Training crawlers and live-answer crawlers are different products; treating them the same is a business decision, not a default. Keep a living robots.txt with comments # Policy review: 2026-11-01 # GPTBot: allow public docs + blog only User-agent: GPTBot Allow: /blog/ Allow: /docs/ Disallow: / Comments with a review date stop the file becoming archaeology. Test after every CDN or WAF change Rules at the edge can override origin robots.txt. After a Cloudflare or similar change, curl the live robots.txt and hit a sample of URLs with the relevant user-agent. Log the results next to the matrix. Revisit quarterly New bots appear. Old ones rebrand. Put a calendar reminder. The matrix is only useful if someone owns it. Practical checklist Before you ship the change, walk through a short checklist with someone who did not write the page. Ask them to explain the offer, the price or fee range, the timeline and the main risk in their own words. If they cannot, the draft is not ready for assistants or for humans either. Document the owner of the page, the next review date and the source of every number you quote. When a platform policy or a fee changes, you want a single place to update rather than a scavenger hunt across blog posts, help articles and sales decks. Common failure modes Teams usually fail in three ways. They publish once and never revisit dates. They keep conflicting facts on the About page, a directory and a PDF one-pager. They measure vanity traffic instead of whether the answers that matter improved. A lightweight monthly review catches all three earlier than a panicked quarterly audit. Why Hong Kong-based export teams care Overseas ads, multilingual sites, GEO and crypto checkout for overseas merchants share the same underlying need: clear facts, consistent entities and pages that can be quoted without guesswork. title: Price a coding call, then pick the model tier
author: Conor Bronsdon
summary: For a short coding task, price the fast tier and the flagship on the same prompt, then keep the cheapest run that still returns code you would ship. On the pricing Paige Bailey read off the screen, Gemini 3 Flash input was about 25% of Gemini 3 Pro, a bit lower with a large input context, and output was about 25% as well. With thinking set to minimal, Flash wrote a lat/long helper in about one tenth the time, and the call came in at less than a penny. Paige Bailey is the AI developer relations lead at Google DeepMind. The episode aired in January 2026. She opened compare mode in AI Studio and ran one Python prompt on Gemini 3 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash. How do you choose a model tier for a short coding task? Run the task on the fast tier with thinking turned down, run it on the flagship, and keep the cheaper result that matches the code you wanted. Bailey framed Gemini 3 Pro as the flagship, with thinking built in, a larger model, and a much higher price. Gemini 3 Flash can turn thinking on, at what she called a significant discount next to Pro. In that compare Pro's thinking level was high by default, and she set Flash to minimal. The prompt asked for a Python function that returns lat/long for a city. Flash returned while Pro was still thinking. Sources were cited, both answers used GeoPy, and she called the Python more or less the same. That output had no example usage. For folks who can't see, the input is about 25% of what you would expect to pay for Gemini three Pro, even a little bit lower if you have significant number of tokens in your context window for inputs. And then the output is also significantly less expensive, just coming in at about 25%. Paige Bailey, AI Developer Relations Lead at Google DeepMind, on Chain of Thought ep 47 Gemini 3 & Robot Dogs: Inside … - Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering - Apple Podcasts Podcast Episode · Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering · January 14 · 51m podcasts.apple.com Read the current per-million rates, then apply them to token counts from a run of your own. When do you turn thinking on? Leave thinking at minimal when the fast tier already returns the function you needed. Turn it up when you want a fuller answer and you can afford the extra tokens and the wait. Gemini three Pro, obviously, our flagship model. It has thinking baked in, which means that the answers you're going to get are probably going to be much more fully expressed, but they'll probably take a a lot longer to get you the answer that you're hoping for Paige Bailey, AI Developer Relations Lead at Google DeepMind, on Chain of Thought ep 47 On the city lookup, she tied the savings to not using all of the intermediate thinking tokens on that run. Measure the thinking tokens you were billed. Flash still has a switch if a later task needs thinking. Minimal thinking fits a narrow function with an obvious library. Raise it above minimal when the prompt asks for a design, several files, or a justification you will review. One demo where the Python matched does not settle the next prompt. How do you estimate the cost of one coding call? Multiply input tokens and output tokens by the per-million prices you supply for that tier, then pick the cheapest tier that passed a quality check you recorded. On hover, the compare view showed input cost, output cost, and total. The Flash total for that function was less than a penny. The sketch below does the same arithmetic. It takes prices as parameters, so you can pass the card you are billed on. A minimal sketch to adapt, not a drop-in library. def call_cost_usd ( input_tokens , output_tokens , thinking_tokens , usd_per_million_in , usd_per_million_out , ): billed_out = output_tokens + thinking_tokens return ( input_tokens * usd_per_million_in + billed_out * usd_per_million_out ) / 1_000_000 def cheapest_tier_that_passed ( runs , prices ): passed = [ run for run in runs if run [ " passed " ]] if not passed : return None def cost ( run ): rate = prices [ run [ " name " ]] return call_cost_usd ( run [ " input_tokens " ], run [ " output_tokens " ], run [ " thinking_tokens " ], rate [ " usd_per_million_in " ], rate [ " usd_per_million_out " ], ) return min ( passed , key = cost )[ " name " ] Feed it token counts from the two runs, including the thinking tokens you were billed, and the per-million input and output prices from the card you are billed on. Check the billing documentation for how thinking tokens are charged and whether reported output counts already include them. On that compare she tied Flash's lower token use to not using all of the intermediate thinking tokens, and she put Pro's slower answer down to those tokens and its larger size. If nothing passed, the function returns no tier. Change the prompt or the check before you accept the cheap failure. Mark a run as passed only from checks you can rerun. The function should do the job, verified by a tiny fixture you wrote. Dependencies should be ones you will ship. Both of her samples pulled in GeoPy; if that is not a dependency you will ship, both runs fail. Latency should fit the product: about one tenth of the wait matters in an inline editor and matters less in a nightly job. Cost at your volume should still look like that penny-scale call once you multiply by how often the path runs. Those figures come from one prompt, so copy the shape of the test. FAQ Is Gemini 3 Flash about a quarter of Pro on both input and output? On the comparison Bailey showed, input was about 25% of Pro, and lower than that with a significant number of input tokens. Output was about 25%. Confirm the card for the context length you send. Does the fast tier have thinking at all? Pro had thinking baked in, and in that UI the thinking level defaulted to high. Flash let her turn thinking on. She set thinking to minimal for the lat/long prompt. Measure the thinking tokens that call billed. Will both tiers emit the same code? On that one prompt, she said the Python was more or less the same and both used GeoPy. Treat that as a single data point. Keep a fixture so a later prompt can fail the bar even when it is cheap. Takeaway Run one real coding prompt on the fast tier with thinking minimal and on the flagship with thinking at its default. Record input tokens, output tokens, wall time, and total cost from the run. Use about 25% of Pro on input and on output only as the ratio Bailey showed, and pass today's per-million prices into your own estimator. Raise thinking above minimal when the short answer is too thin, and count the thinking tokens you were billed. Ship the cheapest tier that passed your fixture, dependency check, latency limit, and budget. The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought . Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one. Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

title: I built a prize wheel for our perfume shops that only spins once you actually follow us on Instagram
author: Brahim
summary: Result first: customers in our perfume shops scan a QR code on a flyer, follow our Instagram account, type the first letters of their username, tap their own profile picture, and the prize wheel unlocks. The follow check is automatic and takes about 2–3 seconds, even for private accounts that followed a few seconds earlier. The question I was trying to answer: can a small shop check "did this person really follow us?" without asking the cashier to look at the customer's phone, and without the customer logging in with Instagram? What didn't work I was skeptical. The official Graph API doesn't tell you who follows you. So I went through the usual list: Instagram DMs: technically possible, but way too much friction for someone standing at the counter. Logging in with my own account and cookies: fragile, and a good way to get the account flagged. A couple of RapidAPI scrapers: rate-limited (429s), or they return followers in a random cached order, so someone who followed 10 seconds ago isn't in the list. An Apify actor that advertised a query parameter: it returned the same first page whatever I searched for. A SaaS wheel tool: it doesn't verify the follow at all, it just trusts the customer. What worked What finally worked is a "search inside followers" endpoint. I used HikerAPI . You give it the account's user id and a partial username, and it returns the matching followers with their profile pictures. That fits the UX perfectly: the customer types 3–4 letters, sees up to 5 profile pictures, and taps their own. import requests headers = { " x-access-key " : " YOUR_KEY " } r = requests . get ( " https://api.hikerapi.com/v1/user/search/followers " , params = { " user_id " : " OUR_ACCOUNT_ID " , " query " : " brah " }, headers = headers , ) for u in r . json (): print ( u [ " username " ], u [ " profile_pic_url " ]) Setup: a WordPress plugin on our existing site. The call happens server-side only, so the key never reaches the browser, and results are cached for 60 seconds so a customer typing letter by letter doesn't burn a request on every keystroke. In practice it's 2–4 requests per player, at about $0.001 each. Honest limitations The search is partial, so I match the tapped profile exactly on the server. Otherwise someone could type "a" and pick a stranger. It proves the account follows you now . Nothing stops someone from unfollowing afterwards. For a one-shot prize that's acceptable. It relies on a third-party API. If it's down, the game falls back to "show your phone to the seller", which is what shops were doing before anyway. I wouldn't use this to collect data. We only store the username and the result of the check. Curious whether others have solved "verify a social action" for in-store promos differently, especially without Instagram login. Did anyone find something lighter than this?

title: title: "What Happens When Code Changes, But the Docs Don't? How We Built Docs-Drive at Hacktoberfest Hack Day" published: true
author: Sahaj Choukhani
summary: description: "How we built an offline tool, GitHub Action, and web dashboard that catches outdated documentation before a Pull Request gets merged." Every year during Hacktoberfest, developers spend hours exploring open source repositories. You find a cool project, read the setup guide, copy a command into your terminal, and immediately hit an error: bash error: unrecognized arguments: --timeout-secs You check git blame and find out someone renamed --timeout-secs to --timeout in the code four pull requests ago, but forgot to update the documentation. Code changes constantly, but documentation is usually updated by hand. When code and documentation don't match anymore, it creates a roadblock for new contributors and extra work for maintainers. At Hacktoberfest Hack Day at Rishihood University, our team wanted to solve this problem. We built Docs-Drive, a tool that checks code changes against documentation automatically and tells you exactly what needs to be fixed. The Problem with Just Using an LLM When people first think about solving this problem, they often suggest throwing the whole code diff and the entire documentation folder into an AI model. In practice, that approach runs into three big issues: Too Much Noise: A normal code cleanup or internal rename will trigger dozens of false alarms. Speed and Cost: Reading hundreds of markdown files on every single code push is slow and expensive. Missing API Keys: Many open source contributors work on forks where cloud API keys (like OpenAI or Anthropic) are not available in CI secrets. To fix this, we designed Docs-Drive to work locally and offline first, using simple text matching and structural code analysis before involving any AI. How Docs-Drive Works (Step by Step) Our system runs across four main parts. Here is how code flows from a pull request down to a clean error report. Reading Code Changes and Guarding Against False Alarms The system reads unified diffs from local git repositories, patch files, or GitHub pull requests. It automatically ignores build artifacts, lock files, and binary files. It also includes a PR Doc-Update Guard: if a developer changes a command name and updates the documentation in the same pull request, the tool notices that the docs are already fixed and suppresses any warnings. Extracting Code Changes using AST (Abstract Syntax Trees) Instead of treating code as plain text, the engine parses Python and TypeScript code structurally to spot real changes: Renamed options or flags: For example, changing --timeout-secs to --timeout . Changed default values: For example, changing a default timeout from 30 to 60 . Modified parameters: Adding, removing, or changing function arguments. Removed features: Deleting functions or endpoints that are still mentioned in guides. Internal code cleanups that don't affect public behavior are automatically ignored. Parsing Documentation into Sentences The documentation parser breaks Markdown ( .md , .mdx ) and reStructuredText ( .rst ) files down into individual sentences. It keeps track of the exact line numbers, heading titles, and table structures so it can point right back to the exact sentence that needs fixing. Matching Code Changes to Documentation To figure out which documentation sentence relates to a specific code change, the engine uses a mix of: Exact symbol matching: Looking for direct mentions of variable or flag names. Keyword search (BM25): Matching technical terms. Local embeddings: Finding conceptual links using local embedding models or a simple offline fallback when no local AI is running. Turning it into a GitHub Action and Web Dashboard A local script is helpful, but open source happens on GitHub. We wrapped our core engine into a complete product: GitHub Action: Runs automatically on pull requests. Instead of spamming a pull request with 10 separate comments, it posts a single summary table and updates it cleanly using an invisible HTML signature ( <!-- docs-drift-bot-summary --> ). It also leaves native GitHub suggestion blocks so maintainers can click one button to apply the fix. FastAPI Backend & Next.js Dashboard: We built a full-stack web interface where you can view side-by-side comparisons of code diffs and outdated documentation sentences. AI Fix Generator: If you want help rewriting a sentence, you can click a button to generate a clean fix, paragraph update, or a downloadable.patch` file. We also designed the backend to run smoothly on serverless environments like Vercel by switching to synchronous execution when background workers aren't available. Testing and Results We built a historical testing harness that replays real-world code changes and subsequent documentation fixes. Across our benchmark dataset, the tool achieved 1.00 Precision, 1.00 Recall, and a 1.00 F1 score, successfully catching true documentation drift without false alarms on internal refactors. Backing all of this up, our entire test suite currently sits at 75/75 passing unit tests: bash .venv/bin/python3 -m pytest tests/ -v ======================== 75 passed in 1.42s======================== Final Thoughts Open source thrives when projects are easy to understand and contribute to. Documentation is the first handshake a new developer gets when visiting a repository. By automating how we keep code and text aligned, we can save maintainers hours of review time and keep documentation accurate automatically. If you are exploring open source this month, check out how your favorite projects handle documentation—and happy Hacktoberfest! 🚀 HacktoberfestAtRishihood #NewtonSchoolOfTechnology #OpenSource #Hacktoberfest Written by Sahaj Choukhani (Team HisenBugs) for Hacktoberfest Hack Day at Rishihood University

title: Unit-Testing an Hreflang Map Generated From a Spreadsheet
author: Peter Panda
summary: Many multilingual sites still maintain language alternates in a spreadsheet. Generating hreflang tags or an XML sitemap from that sheet is fine — shipping without tests is not. Broken return links and missing x-default are silent until an audit. Treat the sheet as a fixture Export a frozen CSV into the repo. Columns: path , locale , canonical_host . Generation code reads only that file in tests so a live sheet edit cannot flake CI. Assert reciprocity For every URL A that points to B as zh-CN , B must point back to A as the correct locale. Write one test that builds the full map and checks both directions. Fail with the pair of URLs, not a boolean. Assert x-default policy Decide whether x-default is the English page, a chooser page or omitted. Encode that policy in a test so a future edit cannot drop it quietly. Assert no duplicate locale per cluster A cluster of alternates must not list en twice with different URLs. Deduplicate in the generator and assert in tests. Smoke-test a rendered head snippet For three sample paths, render the actual <link rel="alternate" ...> block and snapshot it. Snapshots catch accidental http vs https and trailing-slash drift. Editorial hygiene Keep a living glossary for product names, markets and fee terms so every writer uses the same spellings. Assistants are sensitive to entity drift; so are enterprise buyers comparing three vendors in one afternoon. When you retire a URL, update internal links the same day and decide whether a redirect or a clean removal is clearer for both crawlers and people. Leaving soft-404 hubs in the navigation teaches everyone the wrong lessons. Practical checklist Before you ship the change, walk through a short checklist with someone who did not write the page. Ask them to explain the offer, the price or fee range, the timeline and the main risk in their own words. If they cannot, the draft is not ready for assistants or for humans either. Document the owner of the page, the next review date and the source of every number you quote. When a platform policy or a fee changes, you want a single place to update rather than a scavenger hunt across blog posts, help articles and sales decks. Common failure modes Teams usually fail in three ways. They publish once and never revisit dates. They keep conflicting facts on the About page, a directory and a PDF one-pager. They measure vanity traffic instead of whether the answers that matter improved. A lightweight monthly review catches all three earlier than a panicked quarterly audit. How this ties to pandawm.com work Overseas ads, multilingual sites, GEO and crypto checkout for overseas merchants share the same underlying need: clear facts, consistent entities and pages that can be quoted without guesswork. The implementation details differ by channel; the editorial discipline does not. A fuller implementation checklist lives in hreflang implementation guide . title: Designing Idempotent Webhook Handlers for Crypto Payment Providers
author: Peter Panda
summary: Crypto payment providers retry webhooks. Your handler will see the same payment.confirmed event more than once, sometimes minutes apart, sometimes after a deploy. If fulfilment is not idempotent, you double-ship digital goods or double-credit wallets. Use the provider event id as the dedupe key Persist event_id (or the equivalent) in a unique-indexed table before you fulfil. If the insert conflicts, return 200 and stop. Do not fulfil first and log later. Verify signatures before you parse business fields Check the HMAC or signature header with the raw body. Reject invalid signatures with 401. Only then parse JSON and trust amounts, asset and order id. Separate "received" from "fulfilled" Mark the event received as soon as verification passes. Fulfil asynchronously if your stack allows it, but keep the dedupe table in the synchronous path so retries during fulfilment still no-op. Map provider states to your ledger carefully Pending, confirmed, underpaid, overpaid and refunded need explicit transitions. An underpaid invoice that later receives a top-up is not the same as a new order. Write the state machine down; do not improvise in the handler. Replay a fixture pack in CI Save a handful of real (sanitised) webhook payloads and replay them twice each in tests. Assert fulfilment side effects run once. This catches the obvious race better than a paragraph in the README. Implementation notes Roll changes out behind a staging URL first when the page touches checkout, tracking or hreflang. Capture before-and-after screenshots of the assistant answers you care about, using the same prompt set and the same day of week. Store them next to the content ticket so the next editor inherits evidence, not folklore. If legal or compliance must sign off, put that gate in the ticket template. Skipping review on money, health or targeting claims is how "helpful" GEO copy becomes a takedown request. Measurement Pick five prompts that represent real buyer questions. Score mentioned / cited / recommended each month. Content work that never moves those scores should be redesigned, not repeated at higher volume. Editorial hygiene Keep a living glossary for product names, markets and fee terms so every writer uses the same spellings. Assistants are sensitive to entity drift; so are enterprise buyers comparing three vendors in one afternoon. When you retire a URL, update internal links the same day and decide whether a redirect or a clean removal is clearer for both crawlers and people. Leaving soft-404 hubs in the navigation teaches everyone the wrong lessons. Reconciliation and refund flows that sit on top of these events are discussed in crypto payment refunds and reconciliation . Published by PandaWM , an overseas marketing team based in Hong Kong.

title: I Let Claude Code Write a 20-Lesson Tutorial Course for My App From Its Codebase
author: amer kasem
summary: I build dashboards. Admin panels, reports, forms, the usual things people need at work. Writing them is the part I enjoy. Explaining them is the part I don't. Every project ended the same way: "how do I add a product?", "where is the monthly export?", the same screen share again for each new person on the client's side. I knew I should make tutorial videos, but recording them meant a quiet room, a clean screen, retakes every time I misclicked, and then the next release would make half of them wrong. So I tried something else. I opened Claude Code in my project folder and gave it one prompt asking it to write a tutorial series for the app. It already had the whole codebase in front of it: every page, every button label, every role, every form field. It came back with a series of more than 20 lessons. I imported that reply once into DashCast, the tool I've been building for this, and each lesson became a narrated video with clicks, zooms and subtitles. I didn't record anything. That changed how I think about tutorial videos, so here is what I learned, and what the tool does and doesn't do. The AI in your project already knows your app The coding assistant you already use has read your routes, templates and labels. That makes it a good author for "how to use this" lessons, better than anything looking at your app from the outside. The flow is: DashCast gives you a prompt, you paste it into Claude Code, Cursor or any AI tool opened in your project folder, and you paste its reply back. A series is imported in one step. Rendering still happens lesson by lesson. Your source code doesn't leave your machine. The prompt runs in your own tool, and DashCast only receives the finished lessons. No repo? Start from a link Sometimes the app isn't yours: a client's system, a third-party tool, an old project you no longer have the code for. In that case you give DashCast a link, a test login and one sentence about the video you want. A built-in AI writer explores the screens, writes the lesson and checks each click before you render. It is limited to 3 lessons a day on a free account and 10 on paid plans. A script, not a recording This is the part that mattered most to me. A recorded video is frozen on the day you record it. A lesson here is a script: what the voice says and what happens on screen at each moment. When a button moves or a menu gets renamed, you change that one step and render again. The voice, the timing and the rest of the lesson stay the same, and only the lessons that changed need a new render. If you want finer control, there's a timeline view (the Scene Designer) that shows the narration word by word with the actions on their own track. You drag a click to the word where it should happen. Checking which lessons a release broke After a deploy, there's a "Check selectors" button on each lesson. In about a minute it lists every button and field the lesson can no longer find on the live app. I use it as a quick way to see which parts of the UI a release actually changed, before a user watches an outdated video. Other things I use it for Client handover. Instead of a call after delivery, I hand over a short course with the code: "How to add a product", "How to approve an order", "How to export the monthly report". It's also something you can list in a quote. Release videos. People skip changelogs but will watch 60 seconds of a new feature. There's a "What's new" video type for that. Support answers. One common ticket, one video under a minute, sent as a link instead of a long reply. A launch video for your own product. The "Marketing" type makes a 30 to 60-second video that talks about outcomes rather than buttons. Logins and sensitive data Most of what users need to learn is behind a login. Lessons sign in with a test account before recording starts, so the password never shows up in the video or the narration. Fields like emails, phone numbers or amounts can be blurred. I use a test account with sample data so the videos show what a real user sees without exposing anything real. Languages The same lesson can be rendered in 14 languages: English, Arabic, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Russian, Turkish, Indonesian, Persian, Urdu and Hindi. The clicks stay the same and only the narration changes. Arabic, Persian and Urdu get right-to-left subtitles. Each video downloads as an MP4 with its subtitle file. Chinese, Japanese and Korean narration aren't available yet. Teams On the Pro and Business plans a team shares one workspace with admin, editor and viewer roles. Pro has 2 seats and Business has 5. What it costs Option Price Video minutes Free sign-up $0, no card 10, plus 5 after your first video Minute pack $5 100, valid 60 days Starter $9 / month 300 Pro $19 / month 1,000, 2 seats Business $49 / month 3,000, 5 seats You pay for rendered minutes. Voice, subtitles and languages are included, writing lessons with your own AI tool costs nothing extra, and failed renders aren't charged. Where it doesn't fit It records web apps in a browser. It doesn't do desktop or mobile apps. It isn't for talking-head videos of yourself. If your UI changes completely, you'll still be rewriting lessons. Small changes are cheap; redesigns aren't free. FAQ Do I need video editing skills? No. You describe the video, the AI writes the lesson, and you get a finished MP4 with voice, subtitles, clicks and zooms. If you want to adjust timing, the Scene Designer works like a simple timeline. Does DashCast see my source code? No. When you use your own AI tool, the prompt runs on your machine inside your project folder, and DashCast receives only the finished lessons. You can also skip the code entirely and start from a link to your app. Does it work with my stack? It works with any web app that opens in a browser, whatever it's built with: Laravel, Django, Rails, Node, React, Vue, WordPress and so on. It doesn't record desktop or mobile apps. Can I make videos for a client's app? Yes. Use a test account on the client's app, render the lessons, then download the MP4 files and subtitles or publish them on a page for the client's users. This post was first published on the DashCast blog: DashCast for Developers .

title: Two details worth checking in a paginated ASP.NET Core CRUD
author: Dayer Arturo López Piña
summary: This article was prepared with AI assistance and is based on a local ASP.NET Core and SQL Server demo. The examples are excerpts, not a complete application or a production-readiness claim. A customer CRUD can look complete when creating, editing, and deleting work from the UI. Two less visible details deserve a closer look: what happens when sort values are equal, and what happens when two requests try to create the same email address. 1. Give pagination a fully specified order The demo keeps query execution in an EF Core repository. The application service bounds the page size before passing the query to it: var size = Math . Clamp ( query . PageSize , 1 , 100 ); var q = query with { Page = Math . Clamp ( query . Page , 1 , int . MaxValue / size ), PageSize = size }; The upper page bound keeps the subsequent integer offset calculation from overflowing. Clamping is a contract choice: an API could reject invalid inputs instead, provided that behavior is documented for its callers. In the repository, each supported ordering includes the unique ID as a second key. For example: data = data . OrderBy ( x => x . Name ). ThenBy ( x => x . Id ); var total = await data . CountAsync ( ct ); var items = await data . Skip (( query . Page - 1 ) * query . PageSize ) . Take ( query . PageSize ) . ToListAsync ( ct ); Sorting only by name leaves the relative order of customers with the same name unspecified. Adding the ID gives those ties an explicit order. This does not make offset pagination a consistent snapshot. Inserts and deletes between page requests can still shift records. Count and item queries are separate database operations too, so concurrent writes can make their results disagree. The example does not solve either issue; those requirements would need a separate design decision. 2. A duplicate check does not enforce uniqueness The application checks whether an email already exists before saving. That gives the common duplicate case a useful response, but two requests can both pass the check before either commits. The database therefore also has a unique index on Email. Infrastructure translates SQL Server's uniqueness errors into an exception defined by Application: try { await db . SaveChangesAsync ( ct ); } catch ( DbUpdateException ex ) when ( ex . InnerException is SqlException { Number : 2601 or 2627 }) { throw new DuplicateEmailException ( ex ); } Application handles that exception, and the API returns HTTP 409 for the duplicate email case. Application does not need to reference SqlException or EF Core. There is an important limit in this small implementation: the translation assumes a uniqueness failure during this save means a duplicate email. If another unique constraint is added, that assumption must be revisited to avoid reporting the wrong error. What was checked, and what remains open The recorded local SQL Server test submitted ten concurrent creates with the same email. It returned one 201 and nine 409 responses. The HTTP smoke test also covered CRUD, filters, sorting, and pagination. These are results from a previous local verification, not an independent installation or a complete correctness proof. The project separates domain entities, application services and interfaces, infrastructure implementations, and API composition. That separation makes the SQL-specific translation easy to locate. It does not remove the need to test the behavior against SQL Server. For a small business application, when would you move from offset pagination to keyset pagination? And how do you identify the exact violated constraint when a repository has several unique keys?

title: How we compress a PDF to an exact size in the browser, with no upload
author: Mirza Games
summary: We are Mirza Games, a small independent studio in Dubai (on Google Play we publish as Sezarr). Most of what we build is puzzle games, but one of the most used things on our site is a plain PDF tool: compress a PDF to a size in KB. This post explains how it works, with excerpts from the real code. The problem: "upload a PDF under 200 KB" Job portals, exam sites and government forms love hard limits. "Certificate, PDF, max 200 KB." "Scanned ID, under 100 KB." The person filling in the form has one number in mind, and the file either passes or it does not. Most compressors offer three buttons: low, medium, high. You pick one, check the size, and try again. If "high" gives 230 KB, there is no button for "a bit more". If it gives 40 KB, the scan may be unreadable, and the reviewer rejects it anyway. So we set ourselves two goals: The user types a target (50, 100, 200, 300, 500 KB, 1 MB, or a custom number), and the file comes out at or under it. The output must stay readable. If the target is too small for that, we say so instead of returning mush. Design choice: everything runs in the browser The files people send to these portals are ID cards, mark sheets, bank letters. We did not want them on our server, so there is no server step at all. The page loads a small UI, and the heavy libraries load only when the user picks a file: qpdf , compiled to WebAssembly (from @mssio/qpdf-wasm ), running in its own Web Worker. pdf-lib , for reading and rewriting PDF objects, also in a worker. pdf.js (the legacy build, so older Android Chrome versions work) for rendering pages to a canvas. All three are vendored in the repo, not loaded from a CDN. Our browser test fails if the page makes any request other than a same-origin GET (plus the analytics script and its hits), so "no upload" is checked on every run, not just promised. The trade-off is that the user's device does all the work. A phone with 2 GB of RAM cannot hold a 300 dpi render of a large page, so the renderer caps each page canvas by navigator.deviceMemory : 1.6 megapixels on 2 GB devices, 2.6 on 4 GB, 4.2 above that. A very large page may then render below the dpi we want, and long documents simply take longer. The UI accepts files up to 300 MB, but big files are slow on weak devices. That is the cost of not uploading. Three steps, stopping as soon as the target fits The engine ( compress.js ) tries three steps in order, from least to most destructive. It returns the first result that is at or under the target. Step 1: lossless repack First we try to shrink the file without changing a single pixel or glyph. Two things run in parallel: qpdf with object streams, Flate recompressed at level 9 ( --recompress-flate --compression-level=9 , which also re-encodes some older filters), unused resources and the XMP metadata stream removed; and a plain pdf-lib re-save. The smaller one wins. // 1. lossless let base = { bytes : orig , size : orig . length }; const tries = await Promise . allSettled ([ qpdfOptimize ( orig . slice ()), run ( ' resave ' , [ orig . slice ()])]); for ( const t of tries ) if ( t . status === ' fulfilled ' && t . value . length < base . size ) base = { bytes : t . value , size : t . value . length }; check (); if ( base . size <= target ) return { bytes : base . bytes , size : base . size , step : ' lossless ' , floor : false }; const candidates = [{ bytes : base . bytes , size : base . size , step : ' lossless ' }]; // legible results, for the floor case Promise.allSettled matters: if one tool chokes on a strange file, the other can still win. Note the candidates list too. Every readable result is kept, because we may need the smallest of them later. Step 2: re-encode only the embedded images If the file is still too big, the weight is almost always in images: a phone photo of a certificate, or a scan saved at 600 dpi. Step 2 touches only those images. Text, fonts and vector drawings stay exactly as they were. pdf-lib lists the image objects we can safely rewrite: 8-bit RGB or grey, JPEG or Flate (with PNG predictors undone in the browser), and no masks or Decode arrays. Anything unusual is left alone. For each image we need to know how big it is actually drawn on the page. A 4000-pixel-wide photo shown 3 inches wide does not need 4000 pixels. We walk pdf.js operator lists, track the transform matrix, and record the largest size each image is painted at. Then each image is offered at a few (dpi, JPEG quality) options: export const IMAGE_OPTS = [[ 200 , 0.82 ], [ 150 , 0.82 ], [ 150 , 0.68 ], [ 120 , 0.78 ], [ 120 , 0.65 ], [ 150 , 0.55 ], [ 120 , 0.5 ]]; // photographs (not scans of text) may go a little lower: no text to keep readable inside them export const PHOTO_IMAGE_OPTS = [[ 100 , 0.6 ], [ 100 , 0.5 ]]; // scans of text stay sharp as JPEG only at >= 150 dpi, quality 0.7; below that, step 3's crisp 1-bit pages win export const TEXT_IMAGE_OPTS = [[ 200 , 0.82 ], [ 150 , 0.82 ], [ 150 , 0.7 ]]; A small probe of each image is classified as "text-like" (mostly white paper, very little colour) or not. Scanned text gets only the three conservative options; other images get the full list. Options larger than the original are dropped, and keeping the original is always allowed. Picking one option per image so the total fits a budget is a small knapsack problem. We use a greedy chooser: export function chooseOptions ( sizes , budget ) { const picks = sizes . map (() => 0 ); let total = sizes . reduce (( a , s ) => a + s [ 0 ], 0 ); while ( total > budget ) { let bi = - 1 , bs = - Infinity ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < sizes . length ; i ++ ) { const p = picks [ i ]; if ( p + 1 >= sizes [ i ]. length ) continue ; const save = sizes [ i ][ p ] - sizes [ i ][ p + 1 ]; if ( save > bs ) { bs = save ; bi = i ; } } if ( bi < 0 ) break ; total += sizes [ bi ][ picks [ bi ] + 1 ] - sizes [ bi ][ picks [ bi ]]; picks [ bi ] ++ ; } // ... (if nothing fits, return the smallest option everywhere with fits: false) // fill: upgrade the cheapest steps while the budget allows In words: start with the best option everywhere. While over budget, step down on whichever image saves the most bytes. Once it fits, go back and upgrade the cheapest steps while there is still room. That last pass is what gets the result close to the target instead of far under it. The budget is the target minus the bytes that are not images, minus a rough 160 bytes of overhead per replaced image. The new JPEGs are swapped into the existing objects in place. Because our overhead guess can be off, the engine builds the real file, measures it, and if it is still over, shrinks the budget by the overshoot plus 512 bytes and tries again, up to four times. Step 3: rasterise pages, only as a last resort If text, fonts or vectors themselves are too heavy for the target, the only way down is to turn pages into images. This is the step that loses selectable text, so it runs last, and the result screen says plainly that the pages became images. Each page is rendered with pdf.js at 150 dpi and classified with the same text-like test. Text pages are rendered again at 200 dpi and converted to 1-bit black and white : an Otsu threshold picks the ink/paper cut-off, pixels are packed eight to a byte, and the result is Flate-compressed with the browser's CompressionStream . A crisp 1-bit page is often much smaller than a blurry JPEG of the same page, and much easier to read. Text pages get 200, 150 and 120 dpi options. Photo pages become JPEGs at 150 to 100 dpi, quality 0.8 down to 0.5, converted to greyscale if they had almost no colour anyway. The same chooseOptions picks one option per page: let budget = target - ( 900 + 380 * n ); for ( let attempt = 0 ; attempt < 4 ; attempt ++ ) { check (); const ch = chooseOptions ( pages . map (( p ) => p . opts . map (( o ) => o . size )), budget ); const out = await buildR ( ch . picks ); const minDpi = Math . min (... pages . map (( p , i ) => p . opts [ ch . picks [ i ]]. dpi )); if ( out . length <= target ) return { bytes : out , size : out . length , step : ' raster ' , kinds , floor : false , minDpi }; if ( ! ch . fits ) { candidates . push ({ bytes : out , size : out . length , step : ' raster ' , kinds , minDpi }); break ; } budget -= out . length - target + 512 ; } // Below the legibility floor: the smallest readable file we made. const best = candidates . reduce (( a , b ) => ( b . size < a . size ? b : a )); return { ... best , floor : true }; Floors: smallest readable size beats any size at all Notice that every option list above ends somewhere. There is no "50 dpi, quality 0.2" option. The hard floors are: text pages: 120 dpi, 1-bit photo pages: 100 dpi, JPEG quality 0.5 embedded scans of text: 150 dpi, quality 0.7 other embedded images: 120 dpi, quality 0.5 (photographs 100 dpi) If even the smallest options do not fit, the engine returns the smallest readable file it made in any step, flagged with floor: true . The UI then says "Smallest readable size is X" and names the download ..._smallest_readable.pdf . We learned this the hard way: an earlier version always hit the number, and a text form compressed to 50 KB came out unreadable. Such a file is worse than useless. The portal accepts it, and the reviewer rejects the application later. An honest floor lets the user decide: ask for a higher limit, drop a page, or rescan. How readability is tested. A headless Chrome test drives the real UI. It compresses five generated fixtures (a dense one-page form with an embedded font, a 5-page report, a 300 dpi scan, a photo brochure, a 20-page photo PDF) to 50, 100, 200 and 500 KB. A run passes only if: the output is at or under the target, or the tool showed the floor message; qpdf --check accepts the file; the text stays legible. Original and output are both rendered with pdf.js at 150 dpi and compared only on text windows (small blocks where the original shows dark strokes on light paper). Mean SSIM must be at least 0.7, and edge sharpness (output relative to original) at least 0.75. Those thresholds were calibrated against the old engine: its unreadable outputs scored 0.18 to 0.55 SSIM, while crisp results score 0.8 or more. Unit tests in Node cover the pure parts: chooseOptions (including the "nothing fits" case), the Otsu threshold and bit packing, image listing and replacement, and the 1-bit page builder, whose output qpdf must accept. Units: what is a KB? Portals disagree: some mean 1000 bytes, some 1024. We take the safer reading. A maximum KB is 1000 bytes, so a "200 KB" target means 200,000 bytes, which also passes a portal that allows 204,800. (Our photo tools also have minimum sizes; there a KB is 1024 bytes, for the same reason in reverse.) The result screen shows the exact byte count, so nobody has to guess. What we learned, and the trade-offs "Exact size" really means "at or under". The greedy fill gets close to the target, but we never pad a PDF upward. The point is passing the limit, not hitting it to the byte. Order matters more than clever encoding. Steps 1 and 2 keep the text selectable. Rasterising is easy and tempting for everything; we kept it last on purpose. We skip images we do not fully understand. Masks, Decode arrays and odd bit depths are left alone. Some files then need step 3, but none get a broken image. Size estimates are guesses, so measure. Both the image and raster steps build the real file, check its length, and retry. Client-side has real limits. Speed and render size depend on the device. We chose slow and private. Readability needs a number. "Looks fine to me" did not catch the bad 50 KB form. A metric on text regions, with a threshold, did. Try it The tool is live at mirzagames.com/pdf/compress-pdf-to-kb/ , and the other PDF tools (merge, split, photo to KB and more) are at mirzagames.com/pdf/ . It runs fully in your browser, so you can test it on a real document. If you find a PDF that comes out unreadable, or that should have reached a target and did not, we would like to hear about it in the comments.

title: Ofrenda local: a Día de Muertos remembrance writer that runs offline with Gemma 3
author: Nora Aguirre
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Every year on November 1 and 2, families across Mexico set a table for people who are no longer at it. There are candles, marigolds, papel picado, their favorite food and their favorite songs. The ofrenda is not a decoration. It is a way of saying that someone is still part of the family. Ofrenda local is a small tool that helps you start that table. You tell it the name of someone you miss, what they were to you, their favorite food, a song they loved, a memory, and the tone you want (tender, cheerful or solemn). You can add a photo if you like. A local language model then writes, in Mexican Spanish: a short remembrance addressed to them, a calaverita literaria , the affectionate, playful verse that is part of the tradition, a one-line cartelito for a papel picado or a card, items for the ofrenda taken only from what you told it, and, if you added a photo, a plain description of what is visible in it. It also lists the traditional elements of an ofrenda with their meaning. You can edit everything, copy it, or print a sheet to put on the altar. How I read the theme. For me, a "ghost in the machine" is the trace of a person that stays in the things they leave behind: a recipe, a song, a way of saying something. I wanted a machine that helps you hold on to that trace without taking it anywhere. Demo Code nora-programadora / ofrenda-local Ofrenda local Tell it about someone you miss and get a short remembrance, a calaverita , a checklist for their ofrenda and an image of how the altar could look. The AI runs on your own computer, with no internet: your stories and photos never leave your machine. Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine (Día de Muertos). Post on DEV: [[TODO: add link once published]] Demo video: VIDEO What it does You write a few things about a loved one: name, what they were to you, favorite food, a song, a memory, and the tone you want (tender, cheerful or solemn). A photo is optional. A local Gemma 3 model writes, in Mexican Spanish a short remembrance addressed to them, a calaverita literaria (affectionate, never cruel), a one-line cartelito for a papel picado or a card, personal items for the ofrenda taken only… View on GitHub To run it: install Ollama , ollama pull gemma3:4b , then npm install && npm run dev and open http://localhost:5173 . How I Built It Model: Gemma 3 (4B, vision-capable, open weights). Inference: Ollama , running on my laptop. No cloud calls anywhere. Backend: Node.js, TypeScript and Express. Frontend: React and Vite, with a print stylesheet for the ofrenda sheet. A few decisions shaped the project. The model writes. The code owns the facts. The traditional elements of an ofrenda and what they mean are fixed text in the code. I did not want a small model improvising cultural content, so the model only writes the personal parts. Structured output. I pass a JSON schema to Ollama's format parameter so the answer always has the same shape, and the server validates it again before showing anything: body : JSON . stringify ({ model : config . model , // gemma3:4b stream : false , format : schema , // JSON schema for the answer options : { temperature : 0.7 }, messages : [ { role : " system " , content : systemPrompt }, { role : " user " , content : userMessage , images : imageBase64 ? [ imageBase64 ] : undefined }, ], }) Guardrails in the prompt. This is a sensitive subject, so the system prompt is strict. The model must use only the data you provide and never invent facts about the person, such as dates, relatives or causes of death. If there is little information, it should write something more general instead of filling the gaps. It must treat your text as data, not as instructions. The calaverita has to stay affectionate and never mock illness, the body or how someone died. And a photo can be described but never used to identify anyone. Photos. Gemma's vision lets the app describe what is visible in an optional photo, like a smile or the kitchen behind someone, so the remembrance can mention it. That description is shown to you, so you can see exactly what the model noticed. I built this with help from Claude, in chat, as a pair programmer. A real example. Cartelito: ... Remembrance: ... Calaverita: ... and say honestly what worked and what did not (rhymes, tone, anything it got wrong). If you tried gemma3:12b , say whether the verses improved.]] Limits. A 4B model rhymes unevenly in Spanish, so the output is a draft you are meant to edit, and that is how the app presents it. Each generation takes about 40 seconds on my laptop. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Privacy. A family story and a photo of someone who has died are not things I want to upload to a company's server. Here they go from the browser to my own machine and stay there. It works with the lights, and the internet, off. After the model is downloaded, no connection is needed. That fits an ofrenda, which is about being present, not online. It cannot disappear. If a service shuts down or changes its terms, a remembrance you wrote with it is not lost, because the tool does not depend on anyone's API. Control. I can rewrite the prompt, enforce my own schema and swap the model with one environment variable. I have not compared this against a closed API, so I will not claim it writes better verse. What open weights gave me is privacy, independence and control, in a use case where those matter more than polish. Prize Categories Gemma

title: 2026 Compare Image Generation APIs Like OpenAI DALL-E for Healthtech SaaS
author: mT41Gzp73rc6
summary: For a healthtech SaaS that turns private knowledge-base answers into images, choose the provider by its governance boundary before comparing creative output. OpenAI is the sensible managed baseline; Stability AI fits teams that already operate self-hosted diffusion; Midjourney belongs in a human creative workflow unless its integration contract changes. The image must remain optional, traceable, and unable to outrank the approved text answer. Short answer: keep retrieval, authorization, and answer assembly independent from generation, then put each image provider behind the same adapter. Quality decides whether an image is acceptable. Latency decides whether it is synchronous. Those are related measurements, not one score. This is a small distinction with large consequences. A plausible diagram can still introduce a clinical claim that was absent from the source. A fast endpoint can still be the wrong endpoint for a request that needs a private, reviewable artifact. What must the image boundary guarantee? Start with invariants. The prompt may contain only facts retrieved from the tenant's private knowledge base and approved for the requesting user. The resulting artifact needs a reference to the answer that produced it. Delivery stays private. The generated image is an illustration, never clinical authority. The failure boundary belongs between answering and illustrating. Retrieval, authorization, and answer assembly happen first. Generation follows as a separate job. If a provider is slow, rate-limited, or rejected, the text answer remains available and the image becomes pending or unavailable. That failure mode is appropriate for an educational visual; it is not appropriate to hold the whole answer hostage to a decorative asset. The acceptance gate has two parts: factual alignment and a product latency budget. Check labels, qualifiers, and forbidden additions for the first. Check time to a usable answer and time to a completed asset for the second. I would rather reject a fast image that adds an unapproved dosage than accept it because its request returned quickly. How should we compare image generation APIs like OpenAI? The adapter should accept approved facts and return an image job state. It owns prompt construction, request identifiers, retry behavior, provider metadata, and error translation. The question-answer handler should not know whether the downstream implementation is OpenAI, a Stability AI deployment, or a Discord-centered workflow. Option Useful strength Boundary or limitation OpenAI image generation APIs Managed integration with a comparatively short operational path for a SaaS baseline The application still owns tenant policy, evaluation, retries, and private delivery Stability AI diffusion models Open-source models can support self-hosting and local operational control The team takes on GPU operations, model lifecycle, queueing, and tuning Midjourney A viable place for human creative exploration Its Discord-centered workflow may not provide the direct backend integration a SaaS request path needs Gemini An emerging option worth putting into a controlled trial Pricing and support tiers need clarification before a long-lived commitment This is not a price leaderboard. Token-based pricing, quotas, and support tiers deserve a current review before procurement, but a stale unit-price table does not answer the architecture question. The durable test is how much policy and operational ownership remains in the application, and whether the provider can be removed without rewriting the answer path. There is a control-plane consideration too. Infrai can reduce a particular kind of backend friction by putting multiple capabilities behind one credential and one bill, while keeping a plain, self-describing REST surface. Its public discovery surface needs no key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; that makes it easier to inspect a request contract before a regulated workflow depends on it. For a service that may later add token counting, batch work, or storage around the same private-answer workflow, one consistent surface means fewer credentials and reconciliation points to rotate and audit. The trade is clear: unified administration does not make image quality uniform, and it does not remove provider-specific review. How should quality and latency be tested together? Build a small evaluation set that is deliberately awkward. Include abbreviations, short device instructions, ambiguous questions, long answers with qualifying language, and requests that should produce no image. Record whether required qualifiers survive, whether labels are legible, and whether the artifact arrives inside the image budget. Run the same cases through the managed OpenAI path, a Stability AI self-hosted path when available, and a Gemini trial. Keep Midjourney in a separate workflow test because a Discord-centered interaction is not equivalent to a synchronous backend call. I initially treated the provider as the main variable. The harder variable is eligibility. If an answer contains no approved visual facts, the correct result is no image. That branch prevents a fast model from filling a knowledge gap with something that merely looks authoritative. The answer is not a leaderboard. Keep the textual answer on its own latency budget. Submit generation after answer assembly, return the answer immediately when the product allows it, and attach a pending image job. This makes p95 generation time visible without turning p95 image time into the hidden SLA for every private-knowledge-base question. Can the critical path stay small and inspectable? Yes. The example below uses the verified image-generation route through an environment-provided base URL. It keeps the provider call in one function, sends no hardcoded secret, uses an explicit method, and preserves the provider's error body. The adapter contract can then be implemented against another provider without changing retrieval or tenant authorization. import json import os import random import time import urllib.error import urllib.request import uuid def generate_healthtech_image ( approved_facts : list [ str ]) -> dict : if not approved_facts : raise ValueError ( " An image requires approved source facts " ) api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] base_url = os . environ [ " INFRAI_BASE_URL " ]. rstrip ( " / " ) model = os . environ [ " IMAGE_MODEL " ] operation_id = str ( uuid . uuid4 ()) prompt = ( " Create a patient-friendly educational diagram using only these approved facts: " + " ; " . join ( approved_facts ) + " Do not add diagnoses, dosages, contraindications, or unprovided clinical claims. " ) payload = json . dumps ({ " model " : model , " prompt " : prompt }). encode ( " utf-8 " ) request = urllib . request . Request ( base_url + " /images/generations " , data = payload , method = " POST " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " , " Content-Type " : " application/json " , " Idempotency-Key " : operation_id , }, ) for attempt in range ( 4 ): try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( request , timeout = 30 ) as response : body = response . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " ) if not 200 <= response . status < 300 : raise RuntimeError ( f " image generation failed: { response . status } { body } " ) return json . loads ( body ) except urllib . error . HTTPError as error : body = error . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " ) if error . code != 429 or attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( f " image generation failed: { error . code } { body } " ) from error retry_after = error . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) delay = float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt time . sleep ( delay + random . random ()) raise RuntimeError ( " image generation exhausted its retry budget " ) The idempotency key identifies one logical generation, so a worker retry does not silently become a second operation. A 429 is a scheduling signal: honor Retry-After when supplied, back off otherwise, and stop after a bounded retry budget. Other 4xx responses retain their bodies, which gives an operator the real reason without exposing raw provider details as the user-facing message. The function does not send its authorization header to any returned private asset URL. Asset retrieval belongs to the delivery layer and follows that URL's own contract. Persist the job state before dispatching so a worker restart can distinguish a retry from a new generation. Four attempts. Thirty seconds. Those are application boundaries in this sample, not claims about provider latency; a worker can choose a different asynchronous budget while the answer endpoint returns independently. Why reject a direct provider call in the answer handler? A provider-specific call embedded in the web request saves lines at prototype stage. It also couples answer latency to image latency, hides retry state in a process that may restart, and makes provider replacement a rewrite of the user-facing path. That design is valid for an experiment with no tenant policy and no production delivery contract. It is a weak boundary for healthtech. Self-hosting is not automatically safer or cheaper. Stability AI's open-source diffusion models are a valid choice when GPU capacity, deployment ownership, and model updates are already routine. A team without those capabilities may exchange API integration work for operations work without improving its clinical acceptance gate. Conversely, a managed OpenAI baseline is a poor fit when inference must remain inside an established private GPU boundary. One key and one bill can simplify backend administration, but it cannot remove vendor-specific quality review. The same is true of a unified REST contract: it reduces integration surface, not the need to test labels, qualifiers, privacy controls, and support boundaries for the generated artifact. This is where an independent adapter earns its keep. Decision Use OpenAI as the first managed benchmark, keep Stability AI as the self-hosted comparison when the organization can operate it, and treat Midjourney as a separate creative workflow until direct SaaS integration satisfies the contract. Select the production route only after the awkward evaluation set passes the factual gate and the answer remains useful within its own latency budget. The image is optional. The source answer is not. References MDN: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests OpenAI: Images API guide Stability AI Developer Platform Midjourney: Terms of Service Google AI for Developers: Gemini API pricing
